nameStory: The White-winged Scoter gets its name from the distinctive white wing patches that flash brightly when the bird takes flight or stretches its wings. The word 'scoter' comes from an old term meaning 'to scoot,' referring to how these ducks scoot across the water's surface when taking off. The genus name Melanitta comes from ancient Greek words meaning 'black duck,' perfectly describing these dark-colored sea ducks.
description: The White-winged Scoter is a chunky, heavy-bodied sea duck that's built for life on cold ocean waters. Males are mostly black with bright white wing patches and distinctive white crescents around their eyes, while females are brown with the same white wing markings. These are large ducks, similar in size to a Mallard but stockier and more robust-looking. They're specially adapted for diving deep underwater to feed on shellfish and other marine creatures.

idTips.label: White Wing Patches
idTips.description: Bright white patches on the wings that are visible both in flight and when the bird stretches or flaps while on water - these patches flash like white flags and are the most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Male Plumage
idTips.description: Males appear jet black all over except for white wing patches and small white crescents around the eyes that look like tiny parentheses

idTips.label: Female Coloring
idTips.description: Females are rich chocolate brown with lighter, mottled patches on the face and neck, but still show the telltale white wing patches

idTips.label: Bill Shape
idTips.description: Thick, heavy bill that looks almost swollen at the base, designed for crushing shellfish - quite different from the flatter bills of puddle ducks

idTips.label: Body Profile
idTips.description: Sits low and heavy in the water with a chunky, rounded silhouette that looks almost submarine-like compared to other ducks

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies in loose flocks low over the water with steady wingbeats, the white wing patches creating a flickering effect across the group

habitat: Look for White-winged Scoters in New England's coastal waters, especially in deeper bays, harbors, and just offshore from rocky coastlines. They prefer areas with abundant shellfish beds and are often seen in large rafts floating in protected waters like Boston Harbor, Buzzards Bay, or off the Maine coast. During migration, they occasionally show up on large inland lakes and reservoirs.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in April and May when large flocks move through coastal waters heading to northern breeding grounds. Look for mixed flocks of males in breeding plumage and females.
seasonality.summer: Very few remain in New England during summer, with most birds having moved north to breed in Canada and Alaska. Any summer sightings are likely non-breeding individuals.
seasonality.fall: Migration begins in October with numbers building through November. This is often the best time to see large rafts of hundreds or thousands of birds in coastal bays.
seasonality.winter: Good numbers winter along the New England coast, especially in deeper waters off Massachusetts and Maine. They form large flocks that dive synchronously for food.

funFact: White-winged Scoters can dive down to 40 feet underwater and hold their breath for up to a minute while they pry mussels and clams off rocks with their powerful bills - they're essentially the underwater construction workers of the duck world!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Surf Scoters and Black Scoters, but the white wing patches are the dead giveaway - neither of the other scoters has them. Remember: 'White wings = White-winged' - it's that simple! The wing patches show even when the bird is just sitting on the water if it stretches or preens.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sea ducks,' scoters are still true ducks in the same family as Mallards and Wood Ducks - they've just specialized for ocean life. The species is named after French ornithologist Côme-Damien Degland, though most birdwatchers focus more on those unmistakable white wing patches than the scientific naming!
compareHints: Among the three scoter species in New England, White-winged Scoters are the only ones with white wing patches - Surf Scoters have white head patches on males but dark wings, while Black Scoters are entirely dark except for bright orange-yellow bills on males. White-winged Scoters are also the largest of the three scoter species and tend to feed in slightly deeper water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the three scoter species, Surf Scoters are the 'middle child' - larger than Black Scoters but smaller than White-winged Scoters.
Among New England's three scoter species, Black Scoters are the 'plain' ones - males lack the bold white patches of White-winged Scoters and the colorful facial patterns of Surf Scoters.
